title: The Pont du Gard carried water across 456 m while dropping just 2.5 cm

cover.alt: The three tiers of stone arches of the Pont du Gard aqueduct crossing the Gardon river in southern France.

body: The **Pont du Gard** in southern France is a Roman aqueduct bridge 48.8 m high, built around AD 40–60 to carry water to the city of Nîmes. Across its 456 m length the water channel descends only **2.5 cm**, a gradient of 1 in 18,241. The whole 50 km aqueduct dropped just 17 m from its spring, the Fontaine d'Eure, to the city: an average of 1 in 3,000 and as little as 1 in 20,000 in places. Yet it delivered an estimated 40,000 cubic metres a day, each drop taking nearly 27 hours to arrive. The bridge was built largely without mortar or clamps: blocks of up to 6 tonnes were cut to fit and are held by friction and gravity, and stones left jutting from the faces once supported the builders' scaffolding.

slides.alt: Looking up at the underside of one of the Pont du Gard's great stone arches, with blocks projecting from its face.
slides.caption: Under the arches. The blocks projecting from the stonework once held up the Roman scaffolding and were simply left in place.

slides.question: Across the bridge's 456 m, by how many centimetres does the channel drop?
slides.explanation: Just 2.5 cm over 456 m, a gradient of 1 in 18,241. Roman surveyors kept the water moving with slopes far gentler than a modern pavement's.

slides.label: average gradient of the 50 km aqueduct to Nîmes
slides.text: The route winds 50 km to cover a straight-line distance of about 20 km, and in places the slope is as gentle as 1 in 20,000.

slides.heading: Stone on stone
slides.text: Some blocks weigh up to 6 tonnes, cut precisely so that friction and gravity hold them. Building is believed to have taken about fifteen years and 800 to 1,000 workers. In the Middle Ages local lords and the bishops of Uzès charged tolls to cross it, and UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1985.

slides.question: How are the bridge's big stones held together?
options: By their own weight and friction
With lead poured into the joints
slides.explanation: The bridge was built largely without mortar or clamps. The blocks, some up to 6 tonnes, were cut to fit together and stay put by friction and gravity.
